questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: When deaf children from across Nicaragua were brought together in a new school in the late 1970s, the teachers taught in spoken Spanish and the pupils largely failed to follow. Among themselves, though, the children pooled the home-made gestures each had arrived with, and the younger pupils who joined afterwards produced from that pool a grammar their elders had never used. The language was not taught to them; it was _____ by them.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Almost everything living below the reach of sunlight depends on what falls from above: dead plankton, faecal pellets and the discarded mucus of animals nearer the surface, drifting down in pale flakes that take weeks to reach the seabed. Most of the material is eaten on the way down. What arrives at the bottom is therefore not a sample of the surface but the _____ of it.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Threaten a hagfish and it releases a thimbleful of material that becomes litres of gel in a fraction of a second. The gel is mostly seawater held in a mesh of protein threads, each one finer than a spider's silk and wound in the gland into a tight skein. What makes the defence work is not the quantity secreted but the speed with which the threads _____.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: The Miura fold divides a sheet into parallelograms whose creases run in two directions at once, so that pulling one corner opens the entire sheet in a single motion and pushing it closes the sheet again. Engineers folding a solar array for launch want exactly that: a panel the spacecraft can deploy without a separate mechanism at every hinge. The virtue of the pattern is that its many creases act as one _____.

questions.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “medium” most nearly mean?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Egg tempera dries within seconds and cannot be blended once it is on the panel, so a painter builds a shadow out of hundreds of separate strokes laid side by side. Oil stays workable for days and can be pushed about with a finger. A painter moving from one <u>medium</u> to the other gives up a habit of working as much as a material.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Something occupying a middle position between two extremes.

choices.label: B
choices.content: A means of mass communication such as television.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The material in which a work of art is made.

choices.label: D
choices.content: A person claiming to pass on messages from the dead.

questions.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Leon Theremin's instrument is played without being touched. Two aerials radiate weak radio fields; the player's hands alter the capacitance around each one, and the circuit turns those changes into pitch and into volume. There are no keys, frets or stops, so nothing on the instrument marks where a note lies, and the player has to find every pitch in empty air by ear. Few instruments are easier to make a sound on and fewer are harder to play in tune.

choices.label: A
choices.content: To argue that the theremin deserves to be taken more seriously by composers.

choices.label: B
choices.content: To describe the career of the instrument's inventor.

choices.label: C
choices.content: To compare the theremin with the keyboard instruments of its period.

choices.label: D
choices.content: To explain how the instrument works and why playing it accurately is difficult.

questions.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Painters had argued for years about whether a galloping horse ever has all four feet off the ground at once. In 1878 Eadweard Muybridge set a row of cameras along a track in California and ran a trip wire from the track to each shutter. <u>The horse photographed itself, firing the shutters in sequence as it went past.</u> The plates settled the question in an afternoon: at one point in the stride all four feet are indeed clear of the ground, and gathered under the body rather than splayed as painters had drawn them.

choices.label: A
choices.content: It concedes that the photographs failed to settle the dispute.

choices.label: B
choices.content: It describes the way painters had depicted a galloping horse.

choices.label: C
choices.content: It identifies the location at which the cameras were set up.

choices.label: D
choices.content: It explains the arrangement by which the sequence of images was obtained.

questions.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: At its height around 1100 CE, Cahokia held more people than London did, on floodplain across the river from present-day St Louis. Its builders raised some hundred and twenty earthen mounds, the largest with a base wider than the Great Pyramid's, and they moved the soil in baskets: there was no wheel and no draught animal in use. Within two centuries the site was largely empty, and no single cause of that has been established.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Cahokia declined because its floodplain could no longer feed the population.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Cahokia was the only large settlement in North America before European contact.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Cahokia was a very large earthwork city built without wheels or draught animals and later abandoned for reasons still unsettled.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Cahokia's mounds were built to a plan borrowed from Mesoamerica.

questions.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: The Korean alphabet promulgated in 1446 was designed rather than inherited. Its consonant letters are drawn to show the position of the tongue, the lips or the throat that produces them, and letters for related sounds are built by adding a stroke to a basic shape; vowels are assembled from three elements. The preface states plainly that the aim was a script an unlettered person could learn in a morning, at a time when writing Korean meant using Chinese characters learned over years.

choices.label: A
choices.content: The alphabet's shapes and structure were built deliberately around the sounds they represent and around ease of learning.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The alphabet replaced Chinese characters immediately after 1446.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The alphabet was the first writing system ever devised for a spoken language.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The alphabet's vowels were borrowed from an earlier Korean script.

questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Boateng's argument?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Mosquitoes carrying the bacterium Wolbachia transmit dengue poorly, and the bacterium spreads through a wild population once enough infected insects have been released. Epidemiologist Kwame Boateng argues that the fall in dengue cases after such releases is caused by the bacterium itself rather than by the drop in mosquito numbers that the releases also produced.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Wolbachia spreads to a majority of the wild population within a year of release.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Dengue is transmitted only by mosquitoes of the genus Aedes.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Neighbourhoods where mosquito numbers fell by the same amount without any release saw no comparable fall in dengue cases.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Dengue cases fell in every neighbourhood where infected mosquitoes were released.

questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Villalobos's argument?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Airborne lidar strips the forest canopy out of the resulting image and shows the ground beneath it. Surveys of the Petén lowlands have revealed causeways, field walls and house platforms across country mapped for decades as empty forest. Archaeologist Rosa Villalobos argues that the population of the region has been badly underestimated, rather than that the newly visible features belong to a later period than the known centres.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Some of the field walls stand less than a metre high.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Test excavations on the newly detected house platforms recover pottery of the same periods as the pottery from the long-known city centres.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Lidar detects features under canopy that ground survey would take years to find.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The causeways run between centres that were already known to archaeologists.

questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Oyelaran's argument?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Glacial deposits of about 635 million years ago are found on every continent, including several that lay at the equator at the time. Directly above them, worldwide, lies a distinctive layer of carbonate rock tens of metres thick. Geologist Hana Oyelaran argues that this cap carbonate records a rapid end to a global glaciation rather than the slow, piecemeal retreat of separate ice sheets.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Glacial deposits of this age are found on every continent.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Carbonate rock forms readily in warm, shallow seas.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The carbonate layer is thickest in sections that lay closest to the equator.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The cap carbonate rests straight on the glacial deposits everywhere it occurs, with no weathered surface and no gap in deposition between the two.

questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: The pneumatic tube networks that carried letters beneath several European cities charged by the canister rather than by the mile, and a canister crossed a capital in minutes at any hour of the day. The tubes were shut down in the 1980s. What ended them was not that anything faster had appeared on the streets above, since the traffic there had only grown worse, but that the messages themselves _____

choices.label: A
choices.content: were now sent at night rather than by day.

choices.label: B
choices.content: cost more to write than they did to deliver.

choices.label: C
choices.content: had become too heavy for the canisters.

choices.label: D
choices.content: no longer had to be carried as objects at all.

questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Settlers reaching the treeless grassland found no timber within a hundred miles and no money to freight any in. They cut the turf itself into blocks and laid them like masonry, roofing the result with more turf over whatever poles could be found. The walls stood two feet thick and cost nothing but labour. That such houses were built by families who had put up timber houses elsewhere suggests that the choice of material was governed by _____

choices.label: A
choices.content: what the site itself could supply.

choices.label: B
choices.content: building regulations in force on the grassland.

choices.label: C
choices.content: the speed with which turf could be cut.

choices.label: D
choices.content: a preference for the appearance of turf.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: A rider on the Mongol relay carried a message only as far as the next station. Because fresh horses, food and a bed waited at intervals of a day's ride the whole way from the Danube to _____ could travel at a speed no single horse and no single rider could have sustained.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: The pyramids at Meroe are steeper and very much smaller than the Egyptian ones, and there are a great many more of them. Meroe, the capital of the kingdom of Kush for some six hundred _____ over two hundred of them along a few kilometres of desert.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Steel had been made in crucibles a few pounds at a time and cost accordingly. Henry Bessemer found that blowing cold air up through molten pig iron burns out the carbon and raises the temperature of the charge rather than lowering _____ of thirty tons could be blown in twenty minutes with no fuel under it at all.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: A drummer on a talking drum reproduces the tone pattern of speech rather than a code agreed in advance. Because the spoken language is itself tonal, a phrase beaten out on the drum — the pitch, the rhythm, the length of every _____ is recognisable to a listener who has never learned a drum alphabet of any kind.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: The beacons are inspected once a quarter, and a light that fails between inspections is usually reported by the fishing boats before anyone ashore has noticed. Each of the nine beacons on the estuary _____ its own solar panel and a battery sized to carry it through a fortnight of cloud.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Two gauges record the salinity of the same estuary, one at the mouth and one six miles upstream. The salinity measured at the mouth in August is nearly twice _____ recorded at the upstream gauge in the same month.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Three tracks cross the ridge, and the two western ones carry walkers all summer. Of the three, the eastern track is the _____, which is why the estate keeps it clear for the shepherds and lets the others go back to grass.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Nightingale's report set out the mortality figures for the army hospitals month by month, and the columns of numbers went to men who had every reason not to read them. She drew the same figures as wedges of a circle, one wedge to a month, with the area of each wedge standing for the deaths and the deaths from preventable disease shaded separately. _____ a reader who would never have worked through the table could see at a glance that most of the dead had been killed by something other than wounds.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: An electric pump raises water for as long as it is supplied with power, and a village on a hillside with no grid connection gets nothing out of one. A hydraulic ram uses the momentum of falling water to lift a fraction of that water higher than it started, and it has two moving parts and no external supply of any kind. _____ a ram installed on a stream runs unattended for years at the cost of an occasional valve.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: An antlion larva digs a pit in loose sand and waits at the bottom of it. The slope is cut as steep as the sand will hold, so that an ant walking over the rim starts a small slide it cannot climb out of, and the larva throws up more sand to keep the slide going. _____ a trapdoor spider sinks a burrow with a hinged lid that it holds shut from below, letting the ground itself do the work of concealment.

questions.stem: The student wants to explain how a single voice produces two parts at once. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • A throat singer sounds a low drone and a whistling melody at the same time.
  • The melody is made of overtones already present in the drone, not of a second note.
  • Changing the shape of the mouth and tongue strengthens one overtone and damps the rest.
  • The styles are named for the herding landscape: rivers, wind, animals.
  • Herders sing while riding, without any accompaniment.

choices.label: A
choices.content: A throat singer sounds a low drone and a whistling melody at the same time.

choices.label: B
choices.content: By reshaping the mouth and tongue the singer strengthens one of the overtones already contained in the drone and damps the others, so the melody is drawn out of the drone rather than sung separately.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The styles are named for the rivers, wind and animals of the herding landscape.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Herders sing while riding, without any accompaniment.

questions.stem: The student wants to emphasise a difficulty that the recovery programme has had to work around. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • The kakapo is a flightless, nocturnal parrot found only in New Zealand.
  • By 1995 only 51 birds were known to survive.
  • Females breed only in years when the rimu tree fruits heavily, which happens every two to four years.
  • Every living bird wears a transmitter and has a file of its own.
  • Supplementary feeding was found to raise the proportion of male chicks, and the feeding was changed.

choices.label: A
choices.content: The kakapo is a flightless, nocturnal parrot found only in New Zealand, and by 1995 only 51 birds were known to survive.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Because females breed only in the years when the rimu fruits heavily, the programme can add chicks only once every two to four years.

choices.label: C
choices.content: By 1995 only 51 kakapo were known to survive.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Every living kakapo wears a transmitter and has a file of its own.

questions.stem: The student wants to explain how the scale made log entries comparable between one ship and another. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • Before 1805 ships' logs described the wind in whatever words each captain chose.
  • Francis Beaufort defined thirteen numbered forces.
  • Each force was defined by the sail a full-rigged ship could carry in it, not by a measured speed.
  • The scale was made compulsory in Royal Navy logs in 1838.
  • Speeds in miles per hour were attached to the forces only in the twentieth century.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Before 1805 ships' logs described the wind in whatever words each captain chose.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Francis Beaufort defined thirteen numbered forces, and the scale became compulsory in Royal Navy logs in 1838.

choices.label: C
choices.content: By defining each force by the sail a full-rigged ship could carry in it, the scale replaced each captain's private wording with a standard that any other captain could read.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Speeds in miles per hour were attached to the forces only in the twentieth century.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Phages are viruses that attack bacteria and nothing else, and each kind attacks a narrow range of hosts. That narrowness was a drawback when antibiotics arrived: a drug that works against many species is far easier to prescribe than a virus that has to be matched to the strain in front of you. As resistance spreads, the same _____ is being reconsidered as a virtue, since a phage leaves the rest of a patient's bacteria alone.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Ndebele women paint the outside walls of their houses in blocks of colour bounded by black lines, and the whole surface is renewed after the rains. Early photographs show earth pigments in a narrow range of ochres; since commercial paint became available the palette has widened without the geometry changing at all. The tradition has proved _____ about materials while remaining exact about form.

questions.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “burden” most nearly mean?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: The collector wrote down thirty versions of the same ballad in a single valley, and the verses differ from village to village: a name changes, a stanza drops out, a rival suitor appears from nowhere. What holds the versions together is the <u>burden</u> — the line sung after every stanza, which the whole room joins in even when only one singer knows how the story ends.

choices.label: A
choices.content: A heavy load carried with difficulty.

choices.label: B
choices.content: A line repeated after each stanza of a song.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The main point of an argument.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Several orchestras began seating candidates behind a screen in the 1970s, and some asked them to take off their shoes so that a heel on the boards would not give anything away. The change was made to keep the panel's attention on the sound. Whatever else the screen did, it made the judgement _____ of everything about a player that could be seen.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: A badgir is a shaft raised above the roof with openings on one or more of its faces. Air entering the shaft is drawn down through the rooms below and out again, and where the shaft passes over an underground channel of water the air arrives cooled. The tower has no moving parts and consumes nothing, so a house fitted with one stays tolerable through the afternoon at no _____ cost.

questions.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Early train brakes were applied by hand, one carriage at a time, and a driver whistling for brakes could only hope the brakemen heard him. George Westinghouse ran a pipe of compressed air the length of the train. <u>His crucial decision was to let the pressure hold the brakes off rather than push them on.</u> A hose that bursts, a coupling that parts, a carriage that breaks loose — each of these drops the pressure, and each therefore stops the train instead of leaving it to run on unbraked.

choices.label: A
choices.content: It gives the reason compressed air was chosen in preference to steam.

choices.label: B
choices.content: It concedes a weakness in the system that was never resolved.

choices.label: C
choices.content: It identifies the design choice whose consequences the rest of the text spells out.

choices.label: D
choices.content: It describes the hand-braking practice that the new system replaced.

questions.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: The stand of aspen in Utah known as Pando covers forty hectares and looks like a wood. <u>Every trunk in it has grown from one root system and carries the same genes, so the stand is a single organism rather than a population of them.</u> An individual trunk lives perhaps a hundred and fifty years; the roots beneath them are older than any trunk by a wide margin, and put up replacements as the old ones die.

choices.label: A
choices.content: It states the fact about the stand that the rest of the text goes on to develop.

choices.label: B
choices.content: It questions whether the trunks are genetically identical.

choices.label: C
choices.content: It explains why aspen trunks are comparatively short-lived.

choices.label: D
choices.content: It compares Pando with other very large organisms.

questions.stem: According to the text, what happens to the female wasp that enters a fig?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: A fig is not a fruit but a chamber of flowers turned inward. A female wasp forces her way in through a passage so narrow that she loses her wings and often her antennae doing it, lays her eggs, pollinates the flowers and dies inside. The wasps that hatch mate in the dark; the males chew an exit and never leave the tree, while the new females fly off carrying pollen to another fig. Neither the tree nor the insect has any other way of reproducing.

choices.label: A
choices.content: She chews an exit for the males that hatch from her eggs.

choices.label: B
choices.content: She mates inside the fig before she enters it.

choices.label: C
choices.content: She leaves the fig after laying her eggs and carries pollen to another tree.

choices.label: D
choices.content: She is injured entering, lays her eggs, pollinates the flowers and dies inside.

questions.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Parchment was expensive enough to be worth reusing. A scribe in 1229 scraped the ink from a much older book of mathematics, cut the leaves down, turned them and copied a prayer book onto them. The older text was not removed so much as thinned: iron in the original ink had bitten into the skin and stayed there. X-ray fluorescence, which maps that iron without touching the page, has recovered most of the earlier writing from beneath the prayers.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Parchment was reused because scribes disapproved of mathematical writing.

choices.label: B
choices.content: X-ray fluorescence has been used to establish the age of the parchment.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Traces of the original ink survived the scraping and have been read by mapping the iron they left behind.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The prayer book copied in 1229 is of greater historical value than the mathematics beneath it.

questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Ferreira's argument?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Fungal threads link the roots of neighbouring trees, and carbon labelled in one tree can later be detected in another. Ecologist Tomás Ferreira argues that the carbon is moved by the fungus for its own use rather than passed deliberately from tree to tree.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Most of the labelled carbon stays in the fungal tissue itself, and the small amount reaching the second tree arrives whether or not that tree is short of carbon.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Carbon labelled in one tree can be detected in a neighbour within a few days.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Seedlings growing near a large tree survive better than seedlings growing in the open.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The fungal threads link trees of different species as well as trees of the same species.

questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Achebe's argument?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: In a rotating savings club, a fixed group of members pays the same sum into a pot at every meeting and each member in turn takes the whole pot away. Economist Ndidi Achebe argues that what keeps a member who has already taken the pot from walking away is that member's standing among the others rather than any penalty that could be enforced.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Clubs are commonest in districts where bank branches are few.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The order in which members take the pot is usually settled by lot.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Default is rarest in clubs whose members are neighbours or worship together, and no club in the sample has ever recovered money through a court.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Members who take the pot early gain more from the arrangement than those who take it late.

questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Sølve's argument?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: An elephantnose fish emits a weak electrical pulse and senses the distortion that nearby objects impose on the field it creates. Zoologist Ingrid Sølve argues that the fish uses these pulses to locate objects around it rather than solely to signal to other fish.

choices.label: A
choices.content: A fish alone in a tank raises its pulse rate sharply when an unfamiliar object is lowered in, and lowers it again once it has swum around the object.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Fish of this species emit pulses of characteristic and distinguishable waveforms.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Pulse rates rise when two fish are placed in the same tank.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The electric organ develops from modified muscle tissue.

questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Diatoms build their cases from silica dissolved in seawater, and where they bloom they draw the surface water almost clear of it. The cases sink when the cell dies, and much of the silica they carry down is buried in the sediment rather than returning to the surface. Rivers deliver fresh silica to the ocean at a rate that has been measured. Over the long run, then, the silica available at the surface must be governed by _____

choices.label: A
choices.content: the temperature of the surface water.

choices.label: B
choices.content: the number of diatom species present.

choices.label: C
choices.content: the balance between river supply and burial in the sediment.

choices.label: D
choices.content: the depth at which the sinking cases finally settle.

questions.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Sound travels faster in warm water and faster again under pressure. Between the warm surface and the cold, high-pressure deep there is therefore a depth at which the speed of sound reaches a minimum, and sound that strays above or below that depth is bent back towards it. A low call made at that depth is trapped in the layer and can be picked up thousands of kilometres away, which suggests that the range of such a call depends less on its loudness than on _____

choices.label: A
choices.content: the depth at which it is made.

choices.label: B
choices.content: the temperature of the water at the surface.

choices.label: C
choices.content: the size of the animal that makes it.

choices.label: D
choices.content: the direction in which it is aimed.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Medieval glaziers coloured glass in the pot by stirring metal oxides into the melt, so that a blue was blue the whole way through. Silver stain, which reached northern workshops in the fourteenth century, was painted onto the surface of a finished sheet and fired _____ the same sheet could now carry a pot colour and a yellow laid over the top of it.

questions.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: The first patent for a bar code was granted in 1952 and nothing came of it for twenty years, because no reader cheap enough to sit at a till could make out the pattern. The laser and the microprocessor changed _____ in Ohio scanned a packet of chewing gum in 1974, and the system spread from there.

questions.stem: The student wants to explain how the published reports contributed to the improvement in duty. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • Cornish mines burned coal shipped in from Wales, so fuel was their largest running cost.
  • From 1811 a monthly report listed each engine's duty: pounds of water raised one foot per bushel of coal.
  • The reports named the engine, the mine and the engineer responsible.
  • Average reported duty roughly trebled between 1815 and 1840.
  • Engineers copied features from whichever engine stood at the head of the list.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Because the monthly reports ranked every named engine by the water it raised per bushel of coal, engineers could see which engine was doing best and copy its features.

choices.label: B
choices.content: From 1811 a monthly report listed each engine's duty in pounds of water raised one foot per bushel of coal.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Cornish mines burned coal shipped in from Wales, so fuel was their largest running cost.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Average reported duty roughly trebled between 1815 and 1840.

questions.stem: The student wants to explain why dog teams were used to deliver the serum. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • Diphtheria appeared in Nome, Alaska, in January 1925.
  • The port was frozen in and the territory's only aircraft had been dismantled for the winter.
  • Serum was carried 1,085 km from Nenana by twenty dog teams working in relay.
  • The relay took five and a half days in temperatures near minus 50 degrees Celsius.
  • The last driver arrived with the serum frozen but still usable.

choices.label: A
choices.content: The relay took five and a half days in temperatures near minus 50 degrees Celsius.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Diphtheria appeared in Nome, Alaska, in January 1925.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Serum was carried 1,085 km from Nenana to Nome by twenty dog teams working in relay.

choices.label: D
choices.content: With the port frozen in and the territory's only aircraft dismantled for the winter, dog teams were the sole means left of getting serum to Nome.

questions.stem: The student wants to explain what the experiment demonstrates about the pitch. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • In 1927 Thomas Parnell heated a sample of pitch and poured it into a sealed funnel.
  • Pitch shatters like glass when it is struck with a hammer.
  • The funnel was unsealed in 1930 and the pitch began to flow.
  • Nine drops have fallen since, the most recent in 2014.
  • The experiment shows the pitch to be a fluid roughly 100 billion times more viscous than water.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Although pitch shatters like glass when struck, the drops falling from the funnel since 1930 show it to be a fluid, roughly 100 billion times more viscous than water.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Pitch shatters like glass when it is struck with a hammer.

choices.label: C
choices.content: In 1927 Thomas Parnell heated a sample of pitch and poured it into a sealed funnel, which was unsealed in 1930.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Nine drops of pitch have fallen from the funnel since 1930, the most recent of them in 2014.

questions.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: A yakhchal is not a store for ice fetched down from the mountains. Water was run into shallow trenches on winter nights, in the shade of a wall built to keep the low sun off, and it froze where it lay; the ice was then packed into a domed pit whose thick walls of mud and ash admitted almost no heat, with a shaft above to draw off whatever warmth did accumulate. Ice made in a desert in December could in this way be served in July.

choices.label: A
choices.content: It lists the materials used in the walls in order of importance.

choices.label: B
choices.content: It corrects a likely assumption, describes the actual process, and states the outcome.

choices.label: C
choices.content: It presents two rival explanations of the structure and endorses one of them.

choices.label: D
choices.content: It traces the spread of the technique from one region to another.

questions.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: A cyanotype needs no camera. Paper brushed with two iron salts and dried in the dark turns deep blue where light falls on it and stays white wherever something has lain on the surface. Anna Atkins laid dried algae on such paper and set it out in the sun, and from 1843 she issued the results in parts, with handwritten captions, as a book. It is the earliest book known to be illustrated with photographs, and it was made because engraving could not render a specimen of algae accurately enough for the botanists who needed it.

choices.label: A
choices.content: To describe a photographic process and the botanical purpose to which it was first put.

choices.label: B
choices.content: To argue that Atkins has been unfairly overlooked in histories of photography.

choices.label: C
choices.content: To explain the chemistry by which iron salts change colour in sunlight.

choices.label: D
choices.content: To compare cyanotypes with the engravings that botanists had used before.

questions.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Bar-headed geese cross the Himalaya twice a year, at heights where the air holds less than half the oxygen available at sea level. Their haemoglobin takes up oxygen more readily than that of related lowland geese, their lungs are proportionally larger, and the capillaries running through their flight muscle are packed more densely. None of this is switched on for the journey: birds hatched and kept at sea level show the same features.

choices.label: A
choices.content: The birds' flight muscle grows denser capillaries during the migration itself.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The geese are equipped for high flight by inherited traits rather than by changes brought on by the journey.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The geese cross the Himalaya at greater heights than any other bird.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Lowland geese could make the same crossing if they were trained for it.

questions.stem: According to the text, why had Ohio farmers previously fed surplus wheat to their pigs?

questions.passage: Before 1825 a ton of flour cost about a hundred dollars to move from Buffalo to New York City and took three weeks by wagon. The canal that opened that year cut the charge to under ten dollars and the journey to eight days. Farmers in Ohio who had been feeding surplus wheat to their pigs, because the grain would not repay the cost of carriage, began shipping it east instead; within fifteen years the tolls had repaid the whole cost of construction.

choices.label: A
choices.content: The wheat they grew was of too poor a quality to sell in the east.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Moving the wheat to market cost more than the wheat would fetch there.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Pigs were worth more in eastern markets than grain was.

choices.label: D
choices.content: There were too few wagons available to carry the wheat east.

questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Haas's argument?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: A dead whale sinking to the abyssal floor supports a succession of animals for decades, several of which are known from nowhere else. Biologist Meret Haas argues that these specialists move from one carcass to the next rather than persisting at a single site.

choices.content: Bone-eating worms are among the last animals to colonise a carcass.

choices.label: D

questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Pryce's argument?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Until the 1840s a British town set its clocks by the sun, and Bristol ran some ten minutes behind London. Historian Alun Pryce argues that the adoption of a single national time was driven by the railway timetable rather than by the electric telegraph, which came into use at about the same period.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Bristol lies far enough west of London for the difference between them to be noticeable.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Railway companies had imposed London time along their lines several years before the telegraph reached most of the towns on those lines.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The telegraph allowed a time signal to be sent from Greenwich to a distant town in an instant.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Some town councils resisted the change and kept their own time for years afterwards.

questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Sartori's argument?
questions.subject: READING_WRITING
questions.passage: Silphium, a plant harvested in Cyrenaica and prized across the Roman world, appears on the coins of the city and then vanishes from the record entirely in the first century CE. Historian Livia Sartori argues that overharvesting rather than a change in climate ended it.

choices.label: A
choices.content: Silphium was valuable enough to be weighed against silver.

choices.label: B
choices.content: No plant matching the ancient descriptions of silphium grows in the region today.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Attempts to cultivate silphium outside Cyrenaica are recorded as having failed.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Roman authors record grazing and root-digging pushed to the very edge of the plant's range in its final decades, while pollen cores from Cyrenaica show no shift in rainfall across the same period.

questions.stem: The student wants to explain the measures taken to keep the marking impartial. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

questions.passage:

choices.label: A

choices.label: B
choices.content: Candidates sat written examinations on the classics and were sealed into individual cells for up to three days.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Success rates at the highest level fell below one per cent in some years.

questions.stem: The student wants to explain why the specimen landed in 1938 was significant. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

  • Marjorie Courtenay-Latimer, curator of a local museum, kept the specimen and sketched it.
  • The coelacanth's nearest living relatives are lungfish and four-limbed vertebrates, not most other fish.
  • A second population was found off Indonesia in 1997.

choices.label: A
choices.content: In December 1938 a trawler landed a large blue fish off East London, South Africa, and a local curator kept it and sketched it.

choices.label: B
choices.content: A second population of coelacanths was found off Indonesia in 1997.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The fish landed in 1938 belonged to a group known only from fossils and believed to have died out 66 million years ago, so a living specimen overturned that belief.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Marjorie Courtenay-Latimer was the curator of a local museum.

questions.stem: The student wants to explain what the axe indicates about the spread of copper working. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

  • It was buried with an axe whose blade is almost pure copper.
  • Copper working had been thought to reach the region several centuries later than that.
  • Lead isotopes in the blade match ores in southern Tuscany, some 500 km away.
  • Hair from the body carries traces of arsenic, a by-product of smelting copper.

choices.label: A
choices.content: An almost pure copper axe buried about 3300 BCE, its blade matching Tuscan ores some 500 km off, puts copper working in the region centuries earlier than had been thought and ties it to a distant source.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Hair from the body carries traces of arsenic, a by-product of smelting copper.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The blade of the axe is almost pure copper rather than an alloy.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The body found in the Ötztal Alps in 1991 dates to about 3300 BCE.

questions.stem: A vertical pole 2.4 metres tall casts a shadow 1.8 metres long on level ground. At the same moment a nearby spire casts a shadow 31.5 metres long. How many metres tall is the spire?

questions.stem: A bindery sews 8 signatures into every book it makes and used 152 signatures altogether. How many books did the bindery make?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A hiker's pack weighs 23 kilograms. She leaves 5 kilograms of supplies at a mountain hut and divides the rest of the load equally among 3 dry bags. How many kilograms does each dry bag hold?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A kayak hire charges an $18 launch fee plus $13 for each hour on the water. What is the total charge, in dollars, for 5 hours on the water?

questions.stem: A community compost bin holds 240 kilograms of material at the start of the season and loses 15 kilograms of it each week. Which expression gives the mass of material, in kilograms, in the bin after w weeks?

questions.stem: A service lift may carry no more than 8 passengers at a time. Which inequality gives all the possible numbers p of passengers the lift may carry at one time?

questions.stem: A tram ticket costs $4. A traveller pays with a $50 note and receives $14 in change. How many tram tickets did the traveller buy?

questions.stem: On a long drive the function \(D(t)=560-70t\) gives the distance remaining, in kilometres, t hours after the drive begins. What is the meaning of 70 in this model?
questions.subject: MATH

choices.label: A
choices.content: The total distance, in kilometres, of the drive.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The number of hours the whole drive takes.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The distance remaining, in kilometres, one hour after the drive begins.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The number of kilometres by which the remaining distance decreases each hour.

questions.stem: A signwriter uses \(5m-8\) grams of gold leaf on the letters of a sign and \(3m+14\) grams on the border, where m is the number of letters. Which expression gives the total mass of gold leaf, in grams, used on the sign?

questions.stem: A tiler lays \(3(2x+5)\) tiles along one wall of a bathroom. Which expression is equivalent to that number of tiles?

questions.stem: A tiling pattern grows so that the nth figure in the pattern uses \(3n^{2}\) tiles. How many tiles does the 4th figure use?

questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A photographer's exposure index is given by \(g(x)=\frac{x+9}{x-1}\), where x is the meter reading and \(x>1\). What is the exposure index when the meter reading is 5?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A decorator mixes paint using 3 parts white to 5 parts blue by volume. One batch uses 45 litres of white paint. How many litres of blue paint does that batch use?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: The number of passengers using a rural bus route fell from 250 a day to 200 a day. By what percent did the number of passengers fall?

questions.stem: A packing crate is a rectangular box measuring 6 feet by 4 feet by 3 feet. What is the volume of the crate, in cubic feet?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A metallurgist writes two blending constraints as \(6x-4y=10\) and \(9x+cy=15\), where x and y are the masses of two alloys in kilograms and c is a constant. Every pair \((x,y)\) that satisfies the first constraint also satisfies the second. What is the value of c?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A barometric altimeter reports an offset \(f(x)\) for a raw pressure reading x, and f is a linear function. The instrument's log records \(f(-4)=17\) and \(f(6)=-3\). For what value of x does \(f(x)=5\)?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A delivery van carries parcels of two kinds. Each parcel of the first kind has a mass of 12 kilograms and each parcel of the second kind has a mass of 18 kilograms, and the van may carry a total parcel mass of at most 960 kilograms. The van must carry at least 30 parcels of the first kind. What is the greatest number of parcels of the second kind the van can carry?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A framer cuts a rectangular mounting card whose length is 3 centimetres greater than its width, and the card has an area of 154 square centimetres. What is the perimeter, in centimetres, of the card?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A kiln controller turns a dial setting x into a firing temperature with \(h(x)=5x-1\), and the energy the kiln then draws at a firing temperature T is \(f(T)=T^{2}+3\). Which expression gives the energy the kiln draws in terms of the dial setting x?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: The clearance between a parabolic arch and the roadway beneath it, in feet, is given by \(c(x)=3x^{2}+24x+50\), where x is the horizontal distance in feet from a fixed marker. Which equivalent form of the expression displays the minimum clearance as a constant or coefficient?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A sheet of tinplate measuring 20 centimetres by 16 centimetres is made into an open tray by cutting a square of side x centimetres from each corner and folding the four flaps upward. The base of the finished tray has an area of 192 square centimetres. What is the value of x?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: The ratio of two cross-sectional areas in a ventilation duct is written as \(\frac{x^{2}-9}{x^{2}+7x+12}\), where \(x>3\). Which expression is equivalent to that ratio?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: The floor of a dry valley is modelled by \(y=k(x+2)(x-6)\), where k is a constant and x and y are measured in hundreds of metres. The model passes through the point \((0,-36)\). What is the least value of y the model takes?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: While calibrating a pressure gauge a technician has to solve the equation \(\sqrt{2x+11}=x+4\). What is the only value of x that satisfies this equation?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A foundry melts an alloy that is 40% copper together with an alloy that is 70% copper to obtain 90 kilograms of an alloy that is 60% copper. How many kilograms of the 70% alloy does the foundry use?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: A university selected 250 of its 6,000 first-year students at random and then randomly assigned each selected student to one of two study-skills programmes. Students who followed programme X went on to score significantly higher on a common end-of-term assessment than students who followed programme Y. Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
questions.subject: MATH

choices.label: A
choices.content: No conclusion about cause can be drawn, because the students were not assigned at random.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Programme X will raise the assessment score of every first-year student at the university.

choices.label: C
choices.content: First-year students at any university will score higher on the assessment if they follow programme X.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Programme X is likely to cause higher assessment scores for first-year students at this university.

questions.stem: A drawing office sets out a right triangle \(JKL\) in which the right angle is at L, so the angles at J and at K have measures that add to 90°. The office records \(\tan J=\frac{3}{4}\). What is the value of \(\cos K\)?

questions.stem: A caterer packs portions into trays that hold 8 portions each and boxes that hold 5 portions each. She must pack at least 60 portions and may use at most 9 containers in all. If she uses exactly 4 boxes, how many trays must she use?
questions.subject: MATH

questions.stem: The mass of a spool of cable is a linear function of the length of cable wound on it. A spool holding 40 metres of cable has a mass of 27 kilograms, and a spool holding 100 metres of cable has a mass of 51 kilograms. What is the mass, in kilograms, of the empty spool?
questions.subject: MATH
